body.heading: Cooking by glow
paragraphs: A toaster has no flame and barely warms the air around the bread. Its elements are wires of nichrome — a nickel-chromium alloy that resists electricity and heats up instead of melting — which glow orange-hot when current passes through them.

The glowing wires pour out infrared radiation, invisible light that the bread's surface absorbs and turns into heat. Both faces of the slice are toasted at once because elements stand on either side, a few millimetres away. The bread never touches the wires; radiation does all the work.

body.heading: Browning is chemistry
paragraphs: The heat first dries the surface, then triggers real chemistry: above roughly 140 degrees Celsius, sugars and proteins in the bread react in the Maillard reaction, creating hundreds of new flavour compounds and the golden-brown colour. This is browning, not burning — burning is what happens if you wait too long.

The inside of the slice stays soft because the radiation is absorbed at the surface and the short cooking time lets little heat soak through. Toast is therefore a gradient: crisp and flavourful outside, tender within.

body.heading: Timing the pop
paragraphs: Classic toasters timed the cycle with a strip of two metals that bends as it heats, eventually tripping the catch that lets the spring-loaded carriage pop up and switches the elements off. The browning dial simply changed how far the strip had to bend.

Many modern toasters time electronically instead, but the goal is the same: guess the moment the surfaces reach the chosen shade. Since frozen, fresh and sweet breads all brown at different rates, even good toasters need supervision — the chemistry refuses to be perfectly predicted.
